lessons.title: Selecting Breeding Stock
lessons.body: To start breeding rabbits, you need healthy, productive parents. Choose does (females) that are at least 6 months old and bucks (males) at least 7 months. Look for animals with bright eyes, clean noses, and no drooling. Check their teethâthey should be aligned, not overgrown. Feel their body: firm, not fat or thin. A good doe has a wide, well-developed belly and at least 8 teats. A good buck has two large, firm testicles that descend by 5 months. Avoid breeding from rabbits that have had repeated litters of fewer than 4 kits, or that have kindled (given birth) with difficulty. In Africa, many farmers use New Zealand White, California White, or local crosses. These breeds adapt well to heat and are good mothers. If you buy from a market, quarantine new rabbits for 30 days before mixing with your herd. Feed them well during quarantine: 100g of pellets per day plus fresh greens like sweet potato vines or amaranth. Watch for signs of illness like diarrhoea or coughing. Only select from rabbits that have never been sick. Record the parentsâ performance: number of kits born, number weaned, and mothering ability. A doe that weans 6 or more kits per litter is excellent. A buck that mates quickly and successfully with at least 3 does is a keeper. Never breed brother to sister or father to daughterâthis causes weak kits and deformities. Instead, exchange bucks with a neighbour every 12â18 months to bring in new blood. Finally, cull (remove) any rabbit that has produced two consecutive litters with stillborn kits or that refuses to mate. Good selection is the foundation of a profitable rabbitry.

lessons.title: Mating and Gestation Management
lessons.body: Rabbits are ready to mate when the doe is in heatâher vulva becomes pink, swollen, and moist. This happens every 14â16 days, but in warm African climates, does may be ready year-round. Always take the doe to the buckâs cage, never the other way around. The buckâs territory makes him more confident. Mating takes seconds: the buck mounts, falls off, and grunts. After that, he may fall overâthis is normal. Leave the doe for another mating 6â8 hours later to increase litter size. One buck can serve 8â10 does. Do not mate rabbits in the hottest part of the day; early morning or evening is best. After mating, put the doe back in her own cage. Gestation lasts 28â32 days, average 31. Mark the mating date on a card on the cage. During pregnancy, feed the doe 120â150g of pellets daily plus unlimited hay and greens. Provide a nest box on day 27âa wooden box 40cm x 30cm x 30cm with soft bedding like dried grass or shredded paper. Keep the cage clean and quiet. Handle the doe gently; stress can cause abortion. Check for pregnancy signs: by day 14, you can feel grape-sized embryos by gently palpating her bellyâbut only if you are experienced, otherwise you may injure the kits. A simple method is to watch for nesting behaviour: the doe pulls fur from her belly and carries straw in her mouth. If she does not kindle by day 34, consult a vet or experienced farmer. In Africa, many farmers use a âmating chartâ to track dates. If a doe fails to conceive after two matings, give her a rest for 2 weeks and try again. Keep records: date mated, buck used, expected kindling date. This prevents inbreeding and missed pregnancies.

lessons.title: Kindling and Newborn Kit Care
lessons.body: Kindling (giving birth) usually happens at night or early morning and takes 15â30 minutes. The doe will pull fur from her belly and chest to line the nest. Do not disturb her. Stay away but check quietly from a distance. If she kindles during the day, leave her alone. After kindling, count the kitsâbut only after the doe has left the nest to eat or drink. Wear clean hands or use a small spoon to move kits. Newborn kits are blind, deaf, and hairless. They weigh 30â80g. A healthy litter has 4â12 kits. If the doe has more than 10 kits, you may need to foster some to another doe that kindled within 3 days. To foster, remove the foster doe from her cage, rub the new kits with her bedding, and place them in her nest. Watch herâif she accepts them, she will nurse them. If she rejects them, return them to the original mother. Keep the nest box dry and warm. In cold weather, add extra bedding. In hot weather, ensure ventilation but no draughts. The doe nurses once or twice a day, usually at night, for 3â5 minutes. You may not see itâthatâs normal. Check kits daily for full bellies. If their bellies are wrinkled, they are not getting milk. A doe with 8 kits needs 180â200g of pellets daily plus unlimited water. Give her fresh greens like carrot tops, kale, or sweet potato leaves. If a doe dies or rejects her litter, you can hand-feed kits with goat milk using a syringe (without needle) every 2â3 hours for the first week, then every 4 hours. Keep the kits warmâa hot water bottle wrapped in a towel works. Kits open their eyes at 10â12 days and start eating solid food at 3 weeks. By 4 weeks, they will nibble pellets and hay. Always handle kits gently and minimally for the first two weeks. Stress can cause the mother to cannibalise or abandon them.

lessons.title: Weaning and Raising Young Rabbits
lessons.body: Weaning means separating kits from their mother. Do this at 4â6 weeks old, when kits weigh 500â700g and are eating solid food well. In Africa, many farmers wean at 5 weeks to give the doe a rest and rebreed her sooner. But weaning too early (before 4 weeks) causes stress and death. Before weaning, ensure kits are eating the same pellets and hay as the mother. Provide a shallow dish of pellets and a water bottle with a sipper. At weaning, move kits to a clean, dry cage in groups of 4â6 of the same size. Do not mix littersâfighting and disease spread. Keep the cage away from drafts and direct sun. For the first week after weaning, feed the same food they had with the mother. Change feed gradually over 7 days. A common mistake is overfeedingâthis causes diarrhoea. Give 30â50g of pellets per kit per day, split into two meals. Add fresh greens like blackjack, amaranth, or sweet potato leaves, but introduce one at a time. Clean water must be available 24/7. Weigh kits weekly. Healthy kits gain 30â40g per day. At 8 weeks, they should weigh 1.2â1.5kg. Separate males from females at 10â12 weeks to prevent unwanted mating. Males can be sold for meat at 2.5â3kg (12â16 weeks). Keep the best females as future breeders. Watch for signs of illness: dull coat, droopy ears, loss of appetite, or diarrhoea. Isolate sick kits immediately. Coccidiosis is common after weaningâtreat with amprolium in water for 5 days. Provide a mineral lick and keep bedding dry. If you plan to sell, market at 3kg for best price. Record weaning weights and dates. This helps you identify fast-growing lines. Good weaning management reduces mortality from 30% to under 10%.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Breeding
lessons.body: Record keeping is not paperwork for its own sakeâit is your memory and your profit guide. Without records, you cannot know which doe produces the most kits, which buck is infertile, or when to expect kindling. Use a simple notebook or a wall chart. Each cage gets a card. On the card write: rabbit ID (e.g., DOE-01), date of birth, parent IDs, and date acquired. For breeding, record: date mated, buck ID, expected kindling date (31 days later), actual kindling date, number born alive, number born dead, number weaned. Also note any problems: difficult birth, mastitis, cannibalism. For each kit, record: birth weight (optional), weaning weight, and any illness. At the end of each year, calculate for each doe: total kits born, total weaned, and average weaning weight. A good doe weans 20â30 kits per year. A poor doe weans fewer than 10âcull her. For bucks, record: number of does mated, number of successful pregnancies, and litter sizes. A buck that fails to impregnate 3 does in a row should be culled. In Africa, many farmers use a simple colour code: green for good, yellow for watch, red for cull. Put a coloured tag on the cage. Keep a monthly summary: total does bred, total kits born, total deaths, total sold. This helps you plan feed purchases and sales. If you have a smartphone, use a free app like âRabbit Managerâ or âFarm Recordsâ. But paper works fine if kept dry and safe. Review records every month. Look for patterns: are more kits born in certain months? Do some does have small litters? Adjust feeding or culling. Records also help when selling breeding stockâbuyers pay more for proven parents. Finally, keep health records: dates of deworming, vaccinations (if any), and treatments. This prevents drug residues in meat. Good records turn a hobby into a business.

lessons.title: Common Reproductive Problems and Solutions
lessons.body: Reproductive problems cost money. The most common is failure to conceive. Causes: doe too fat or too thin, heat stress, or buck infertility. Solution: feed a balanced diet (16â18% protein pellets), provide shade and ventilation, and check the buckâs testicles for size and firmness. If a doe fails after two matings, give her 2 weeks rest, then try a different buck. Another problem is kindling difficulties (dystocia). The doe strains for over 30 minutes with no kits. This happens if kits are too large or positioned wrong. Gently massage her belly, or if trained, assist by pulling kits with clean fingers. If she still fails, call a vet. Cannibalismâthe doe eats her kitsâis often due to stress, lack of water, or a noisy environment. Provide a quiet nest box, plenty of water, and do not handle newborns for the first 3 days. Mastitis (hot, swollen teats) is caused by bacteria. Treat with antibiotics prescribed by a vet, and apply warm compresses. Kits may need fostering. Stillbirths are common if the doe is too fat or has a long kindling. Reduce feed for obese does before mating. Infertility in bucks: heat stress above 30Â°C can cause temporary sterility for 4â6 weeks. Keep bucks cool with fans or wet sacks. If a buck is permanently infertile, cull him. Pseudopregnancy: the doe acts pregnant but kindles nothing. This happens after a sterile mating. Give her 18 days rest, then rebreed. Retained kits: if a doe kindles some kits but stops, a kit may be stuck. Seek help. Abscesses on the reproductive tract: usually from fighting or poor hygiene. Clean with iodine and give antibiotics. To prevent problems, keep cages clean, provide a balanced diet, avoid overcrowding, and maintain a breeding schedule. Do not breed does under 6 months or over 3 years. Replace breeding stock every 2 years. Keep records to spot problems early. If a doe has three consecutive failed pregnancies, cull her. A healthy rabbitry has a kindling rate above 80% and a weaning rate above 70%.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Breeding and Reproduction in Rabbit Farming

In African rabbit farming, reproduction is the engine of the business. A doe that kindles eight healthy kits every 60â70 days can produce 40â50 marketable rabbits per year. A doe that kindles four kits and loses half before weaning produces less than 10. The difference is not luck â it is management. This practical reference consolidates the key technical decisions, benchmarks, and record-keeping habits that separate profitable rabbitries from subsistence-level operations across Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda, and South Africa.

Whether you are a smallholder with five does or a semi-commercial unit with fifty, the principles are the same: select healthy stock, manage mating intervals, prepare nests, monitor kindling, wean on schedule, and record everything. This module gives you the reference data, diagrams, and checklists to do exactly that.

Reproductive Anatomy and the Breeding Cycle

Rabbits are induced ovulators â the doe releases eggs only after mating stimulation. This means a single mating can result in pregnancy, but the timing of mating relative to the doe's receptivity is critical. A doe in heat (vulva pink to red and swollen) will accept the buck readily; a doe not in heat (vulva pale or white) will refuse or fight. Understanding this cycle allows you to plan matings rather than guess.

Key Performance Benchmarks

Table 1 gives the production targets that commercial rabbitries in Africa should aim for. These are not theoretical ideals â they are based on data from functioning operations in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa.

Table 1: Reproductive Performance Benchmarks for African Rabbitries
Parameter Target Acceptable Range Red Flag
Litter size at birth 8 kits 6â10 kits <4 kits
Kindling rate (does kindling / does mated) 85% 75â90% <60%
Pre-weaning mortality <10% 10â20% >30%
Weaning weight (4 weeks) 500â600 g 400â700 g <350 g
Kits weaned per doe per year 35â40 25â35 <15
Re-breeding interval 14â21 days 21â35 days >60 days
Doe productive lifespan 2â3 years 18 monthsâ3 years <12 months

Source: Compiled from FAO, Rabbit Production (1997); ILRI, Smallholder Rabbit Manual (2018); and Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) rabbit extension materials.

Feed and Nutrition for Breeding Stock

Reproduction is nutritionally expensive. A lactating doe producing 8 kits can drink 2â3 litres of water per day and consume 200â300 g of feed. Underfeeding during gestation and lactation is the single biggest cause of small litters, weak kits, and high pre-weaning mortality in African rabbitries.

Table 2: Daily Nutrient Requirements for Breeding Rabbits (per animal per day)
Nutrient Dry Doe Pregnant Doe Lactating Doe Breeding Buck
Crude protein 15â16% 16â17% 17â18% 16â17%
Crude fibre 14â18% 14â18% 12â16% 14â18%
Digestible energy 2,400 kcal/kg 2,500 kcal/kg 2,600â2,700 kcal/kg 2,500 kcal/kg
Feed quantity 100â120 g 120â150 g 200â300 g 100â120 g
Water 0.3â0.5 L 0.5â0.8 L 2â3 L 0.3â0.5 L
Calcium 0.5â0.6% 0.6â0.8% 0.8â1.0% 0.5â0.6%

Source: Adapted from FAO, Rabbit Feeding and Nutrition (2012) and NRC, Nutrient Requirements of Rabbits (2nd ed., 1977).

Selecting Breeding Stock

Selection is the foundation of every successful rabbitry. A doe with poor mothering instincts will lose kits regardless of how well you feed her. A buck with low libido or poor semen quality will waste your time and feed. Select on these criteria:

  • Does: Choose from litters of 8+ kits. Look for calm temperament, good body condition (not fat, not thin), 4â5 pairs of functional nipples, and a history of successful kindling in their dam.
  • Bucks: Choose from litters of 6+ kits. Check for two descended testicles, good body condition, and active mating behaviour. Avoid bucks from litters with a history of kindling problems.
  • Age at first mating: Does 5â6 months (medium breeds) or 6â8 months (large breeds). Bucks 6â7 months. Never mate underweight animals â they will produce weak litters.
  • Record review: Never select breeding stock without reviewing the dam's production records. A doe that consistently kindles 8+ kits and weans 7+ is worth ten does that kindle 4 and wean 2.

Mating and Gestation Management

Always take the doe to the buck's cage. The doe is territorial in her own cage and may attack the buck. Mating should occur within 5â10 minutes; if the buck mounts and falls off, mating is usually successful. Allow 2â3 services in one session for higher conception rates.

Pregnancy diagnosis can be done by palpation at day 12â14. Feel for marble-sized embryos in the lower abdomen. If the doe is not pregnant, re-mate after 7 days. False pregnancy (pseudopregnancy) lasts 16â18 days â a doe that refuses the buck and nests but does not kindle is likely pseudopregnant.

Kindling and Newborn Kit Care

Prepare a nest box 3â5 days before kindling (day 25â28 of gestation). Provide clean straw or wood shavings. Kindling usually occurs at night and lasts 15â30 minutes. Do not disturb the doe during kindling. After kindling, check the nest once â remove dead kits, count live kits, and ensure the doe has pulled fur to keep kits warm.

Kits are born blind, deaf, and hairless. They depend entirely on the doe's milk for the first 3 weeks. A doe nurses only once or twice per day (usually early morning and late evening). If kits are scattered or cold, warm them slowly and return them to the nest. Fostering kits to another doe that kindled within 2â3 days is possible if you mask the scent by rubbing the kits with the foster doe's fur.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Handling Pregnant and Lactating Does

Pregnant and lactating does are highly sensitive to stress. Never handle a doe roughly, chase her, or expose her to extreme heat or cold during gestation and lactation. Stress can cause abortion, cannibalism of kits, or abandonment. Always approach quietly, support the doe's belly and hindquarters, and never lift a pregnant doe by the ears. In hot African climates, ensure shade and ventilation â heat stress above 30Â°C can cause pregnancy loss and reduced milk production. If a doe kindles on the wire floor instead of the nest box, move kits to the nest box immediately and warm them. If a doe cannibalises her kits, it is usually due to stress, inadequate water, or nutritional deficiency â address the cause before re-breeding her.

Weaning and Raising Young Rabbits

Wean kits at 4â6 weeks (28â42 days). Weaning weight should be 500â600 g. Early weaning (before 4 weeks) increases mortality; late weaning (after 8 weeks) stresses the doe and delays re-breeding. At weaning, move kits to a grow-out cage in groups of 4â6 per cage. Separate males from females at 8â10 weeks to prevent unwanted pregnancies.

Provide a creep feeder with a high-protein (17â18%) starter feed from 3 weeks onward. Kits will nibble on solid food from 2â3 weeks but rely on milk until 4 weeks. After weaning, transition gradually to a grower ration (16â17% protein) over 7â10 days.

Record Keeping for Breeding

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Every breeding rabbitry should maintain the following records:

  • Doe cards: Doe ID, date mated, buck used, date kindled, kits born alive, kits born dead, kits weaned, weaning weight, date re-mated.
  • Buck cards: Buck ID, date of birth, number of does mated, conception rate, date retired.
  • Nest box records: Date nest box provided, date kindling, litter size, kit mortality, date weaned.
  • Feed records: Daily feed consumption per cage, feed cost, feed conversion ratio.
  • Health records: Vaccinations, treatments, mortality events, culling decisions.

Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet. In Kenya, KALRO provides free rabbit record templates. In Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development has extension materials with record-keeping formats. The key is consistency â record every mating, every kindling, every death.

Common Reproductive Problems and Solutions

  • Doe not conceiving: Check body condition (too fat or too thin), check for heat signs, re-mate after 7 days, check buck fertility.
  • Small litters: Increase feed quantity and protein before mating, ensure doe is not over-mated, check buck age.
  • Abortion: Usually caused by stress, heat, or disease. Remove the cause, rest the doe for 30 days, re-mate.
  • Cannibalism: Caused by stress, inadequate water, or nutritional deficiency. Provide plenty of clean water, reduce disturbances, supplement with minerals.
  • Mastitis: Swollen, hot, painful mammary glands. Cull affected does â treatment is rarely economic.
  • Pseudopregnancy: Doe nests but does not kindle. Re-mate after 18 days. Do not cull unless repeated.
  • Retained kits: Doe kindles some kits but retains others. Consult a veterinarian; manual removal may be necessary.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Select breeding stock from litters of 6+ kits with calm temperament and good body condition.
  • â Mate does at 5â6 months (medium breeds) or 6â8 months (large breeds); bucks at 6â7 months.
  • â Always take the doe to the buck's cage; allow 2â3 services per mating session.
  • â Palpate for pregnancy at day 12â14; re-mate non-pregnant does after 7 days.
  • â Provide a clean nest box with straw 3â5 days before kindling (day 25â28).
  • â Check nest once after kindling; remove dead kits, count live kits, ensure fur cover.
  • â Wean kits at 4â6 weeks (500â600 g); separate males and females at 8â10 weeks.
  • â Record every mating, kindling, weaning, and mortality event â no exceptions.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Rabbit Production (1997) â Comprehensive free manual covering breeding, housing, feeding, and health.
  • ILRI â Smallholder Rabbit Manual (2018) â Practical guide for African smallholder rabbit farmers.
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation â Rabbit extension materials and record templates.
  • FAO â Rabbit Feeding and Nutrition (2012) â Detailed nutrient requirements for breeding stock.
  • USDA National Agricultural Library â Rabbit Resources â Free access to rabbit husbandry and health publications.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills Course: Rabbit Farming. For the complete course, see the other modules on Housing and Equipment, Nutrition and Feeding, Health Management, and Marketing and Value Addition.

quiz.q: At what age can a female rabbit (doe) be first mated?
quiz.explanation: Does should be at least 6 months old to be safely bred.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a doe is in heat?
options: B) Her vulva is pink and swollen
quiz.explanation: A pink, swollen, moist vulva indicates the doe is ready to mate.

quiz.q: Where should mating take place?
quiz.explanation: The buck is more confident in his own cage, so always take the doe to him.

quiz.q: How long is the average gestation period for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Rabbit gestation averages 31 days, ranging from 28 to 32 days.

quiz.q: When should you provide a nest box for a pregnant doe?
quiz.explanation: Providing the nest box around day 27 gives the doe time to prepare before kindling.

quiz.q: What is a common sign that a doe is about to kindle?
options: B) She pulls fur and carries straw
quiz.explanation: Nesting behaviour like pulling fur and carrying straw indicates imminent kindling.

quiz.q: How many kits can a doe typically raise well?
quiz.explanation: A healthy litter is usually 4 to 12 kits, though 8 is ideal for good mothering.

quiz.q: What should you do if a doe has more than 10 kits?
options: B) Foster some to another doe
quiz.explanation: Fostering to another doe that kindled within 3 days increases survival.

quiz.q: How often does a doe normally nurse her kits?
options: B) Once or twice a day
quiz.explanation: Does nurse once or twice daily, usually at night, for a few minutes.

quiz.q: At what age do kits open their eyes?
quiz.explanation: Kits open their eyes around 10 to 12 days after birth.

quiz.q: When is the best time to wean kits?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 4 to 6 weeks balances kit health and doe recovery.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of diarrhoea in newly weaned kits?
quiz.explanation: Overfeeding pellets after weaning often leads to diarrhoea.

quiz.q: At what weight can young rabbits be sold for meat?
quiz.explanation: Market weight for meat rabbits is typically 2.5 to 3 kg.

quiz.q: Why should you separate male and female kits at 10-12 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Rabbits can become sexually mature at 10-12 weeks, so separation prevents early pregnancy.

quiz.q: What record is most important for predicting kindling date?
quiz.explanation: The mating date allows you to calculate the expected kindling date (31 days later).

quiz.q: How many kits per year should a good doe wean?
quiz.explanation: A productive doe weans 20 to 30 kits per year.

quiz.q: What should you do with a doe that fails to conceive after two matings?
options: B) Give 2 weeks rest and try again
quiz.explanation: A short rest often restores fertility; if she fails again, consider culling.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of cannibalism in rabbits?
options: B) Stress or lack of water
quiz.explanation: Stress, noise, or insufficient water can cause a doe to eat her kits.

quiz.q: How can you prevent heat stress in breeding bucks?
options: A) Keep them in direct sun
quiz.explanation: Heat stress above 30Â°C can cause temporary infertility; shade and ventilation help.

quiz.q: What is pseudopregnancy?
options: A) A doe acts pregnant but kindles nothing
B) A doe has too many kits
quiz.explanation: Pseudopregnancy is a false pregnancy, often after a sterile mating.

quiz.q: What should you do if a doe strains for over 30 minutes without kindling?
options: B) Gently massage her belly or call a vet
D) Move her to a new cage
quiz.explanation: Dystocia requires assistance; gentle massage or veterinary help may save the doe and kits.

quiz.q: How often should you replace breeding stock?
quiz.explanation: Replacing breeders every 2 years maintains productivity and prevents inbreeding.

quiz.q: What is the best way to avoid inbreeding?
options: B) Exchange bucks with a neighbour
C) Use the same buck for all does
quiz.explanation: Exchanging bucks every 12-18 months introduces new genetics.

quiz.q: What should you record for each doe?
options: A) Number of kits born and weaned
quiz.explanation: Reproductive records like kits born and weaned identify the best does.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mastitis in a doe?
quiz.explanation: Mastitis causes hot, swollen, painful teats and requires antibiotic treatment.

quiz.q: Why should you not handle newborn kits for the first 3 days?
options: B) To prevent stress that may cause cannibalism
quiz.explanation: Minimizing handling reduces stress on the doe and risk of cannibalism.

quiz.q: What is a good kindling rate for a rabbitry?
quiz.explanation: A healthy rabbitry achieves over 80% kindling rate.

quiz.q: What should you do if a doe rejects her litter?
options: C) Put them with another doe
quiz.explanation: Fostering or hand-feeding with goat milk can save rejected kits.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a kit is not getting enough milk?
quiz.explanation: A wrinkled belly indicates the kit is not nursing enough.

quiz.q: What is the best way to keep records on a small farm?
quiz.explanation: Simple written records on cards or notebooks are effective and low-cost.
